parts: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, I = q/t, measured in amperes.

Free electrons in a conductor move randomly with thermal speeds, so with no p.d. there is no net current and no magnetic effect. When a field is applied they acquire a small drift velocity v_d = eEτ/m, where τ is the relaxation time. The current is I = neAv_d.
Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature.

Resistance R = ρl/A depends on four things: length, area of cross-section, material (resistivity ρ) and temperature. Resistivity is a property of the material alone, so a wire of length 2l and area 2A has the same ρ. A wire is least resistive when it is short and thick.

Temperature: a conductor's resistance rises as R_t = R₀(1 + αt). A semiconductor's or insulator's resistivity falls as temperature rises. Example: 50 Ω at 20 °C and 50.5 Ω at 120 °C gives α = 0.5/(50 × 100) = 10⁻⁴ per °C.
Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + … (the maximum resistance). Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … For n equal resistors, R_s/R_p = n².
Household appliances are connected in parallel, so each gets the full mains voltage and can be switched independently.
Example: 10 Ω in series with (3 Ω ∥ 6 Ω = 2 Ω) gives 12 Ω, so on 12 V the current is 1 A.
P = VI = I²R = V²/R. A 40 W, 220 V lamp has R = V²/P = 1210 Ω and I = P/V ≈ 0.18 A. A 100 W bulb on 220 V draws 5/11 A, and a 220 V, 660 W heater draws 3 A with R ≈ 73.3 Ω.
A cell's emf E is the work done per unit charge. Its terminal voltage while delivering current is V = E − Ir. Example: 9 V at 1 A and 6 V at 2 A gives r = 3 Ω and E = 12 V.
Junction rule: ΣI = 0 at a junction (conservation of charge). Loop rule: ΣE = ΣIR around any closed loop (conservation of energy).
A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when P/Q = R/S; then no current flows through the galvanometer arm, which can be ignored.
A metre bridge is a practical Wheatstone bridge: R/S = l/(100 − l). With 5 Ω and 15 Ω, the balance point is at l = 25 cm.

Principle: for a uniform wire carrying a steady current, the p.d. across a length is proportional to that length, V ∝ l. At balance it draws no current from the cell, so it measures emf accurately, unlike a voltmeter.
To compare two emfs: E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂. Using the sum and difference connections, (E₁ + E₂)/(E₁ − E₂) = l₁/l₂.
An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and an ideal voltmeter infinite resistance.
